LiteSearch-VL: Small Multimodal Search Agents via
Trajectory Distillation and Synthetic Step-DPO

Saeed Khaki Affiliation: Microsoft AI Email: saeedkhaki@microsoft.com    Nima Safaei Affiliation: Ohio State University Email: safaei.3@osu.edu    Kamal Ginotra Affiliation: Microsoft AI Email: kamalginotra@microsoft.com
Abstract

Multimodal search agents answer visual questions by interleaving image understanding, web retrieval, tool use, and evidence synthesis. Strong systems exist, but in two expensive regimes: proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 and Gemini, or large open vision-language backbones trained with substantial agentic data and reinforcement learning. We ask a different question: when released agent trajectories are distilled into much smaller backbones under a single-node budget, what is actually transferred? We study this with LiteSearch-VL, a low-compute recipe for Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B that uses only released OpenSearch-VL trajectories, parameter-efficient LoRA adapters, and synthetic step-level preferences: DPO on GPT-5-generated hard negatives targeting five local failure modes (premature answer, wrong tool, weak query, repeated query, ignored image). Across 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts on SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini, the dominant effect is behavioral rather than a uniform accuracy lift: full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning transfers the agent contract, taking the 2B model from almost never emitting a usable answer (1,237/1,240 no_answer rollouts) to 28.4% macro Pass@1, matching or slightly exceeding the off-the-shelf 4B base (25.6%). Synthetic preference learning and compact tool distillation act as refinements rather than phase transitions (best 4B configuration: 30.8% macro Pass@1). Finally, a controlled VDR step-budget ablation shows that extra search turns convert abstentions into wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers, identifying answer verification, not search depth, as the next bottleneck for small multimodal agents.

1 Introduction

Knowledge-intensive visual questions often cannot be answered from the image alone: a model may need to identify an entity in the scene, search for external evidence, inspect a crop or an OCR region, and decide when the accumulated evidence is sufficient to commit to a final answer. This has motivated multimodal search agents that interleave reasoning with retrieval and image-processing tools rather than producing a single direct response [1, 2, 3]. The most capable systems, however, are expensive to reproduce: they either depend on proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 [4] and Gemini [5], or train large open VLM backbones with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning.

OpenSearch-VL [3] changed the data landscape by releasing a 36K corpus of tool-interleaved teacher trajectories, an 8K RL prompt set, and a detailed seven-tool environment, but its strongest models are trained in a substantially larger regime than many research groups can access (agentic SFT on 256 H20 GPUs, then multi-turn GRPO on 64 H20 GPUs). This raises a separate question from frontier performance: what exactly do released multimodal search trajectories teach small VLMs? Do they transfer factual search competence, or do they first teach the more basic agent contract—how to format tool calls, use image handles, integrate observations, and stop searching with a final answer?

We study this question in a deliberately constrained setting: starting from Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B, we train only LoRA adapters (vision tower frozen, multimodal projector trainable) on the released SearchVL-SFT-36k trajectories, construct a compact three-tool distilled variant to probe tool-surface complexity, and build synthetic step-level DPO pairs by asking GPT-5 to generate plausible local mistakes at teacher decision points.

Our evaluation covers ten model cells across four short-answer, knowledge-intensive benchmarks: SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini. The clearest result is that SFT transfers the agent contract: the 2B base model emits no usable final answer on 1,237 of 1,240 questions (0.1% macro Pass@1), while after one epoch of full-trajectory SFT the same backbone reaches 28.4% macro Pass@1 and matches the 4B base on the three easier benchmarks. This is not simply a scaling result: the 4B base already follows the contract on many questions, so its SFT gain is much smaller.

The later stages are more diagnostic than transformative: synthetic step-level DPO improves the macro average by +1.0 points on 2B and +1.7 points on 4B, with the largest localized gain on FVQA but a non-uniform effect across domains; the compact three-tool interface reduces performance at 2B, is nearly cost-free at 4B on average, and strongest on FVQA; and increasing the VDR step budget from 5 to 8 reduces no_answer substantially but barely changes Pass@1—the recovered rollouts mostly become wrong_entity, pointing at verification, not search depth, as the remaining bottleneck.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A low-compute recipe for 2B/4B multimodal search agents from released trajectories on one eight-GPU node.

  • •

    Full-trajectory SFT as a qualitative transition (2B no_answer 1,237→\to514; Pass@1 0.1%→\to28.4%).

  • •

    Synthetic step-level DPO and compact tool distillation evaluated as refinements, not phase transitions.

  • •

    A failure-mode and step-budget analysis: VDR is limited by answer verification, not search turns.

We defer a full discussion of related work to Appendix A.

2 Setup and Method

LiteSearch-VL has three stages, described below after the agent formalism; Figure 2 (Appendix B) gives an overview of the full pipeline.

Agent loop.

Given an image I0I_{0} and a question qq, a multimodal search agent produces interleaved reasoning, tool-use, and observation steps culminating in a final answer. At step ℓ\ell the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} conditions on the history hℓ=(ℐℓ,q,𝐚<ℓ,𝐨<ℓ)h_{\ell}=(\mathcal{I}_{\ell},q,\mathbf{a}_{<\ell},\mathbf{o}_{<\ell}), with ℐℓ\mathcal{I}_{\ell} the growing visual context, and emits an action aℓ=[zℓ,cℓ]a_{\ell}=[z_{\ell},c_{\ell}]: a chain-of-thought zℓz_{\ell} plus either a tool call cℓ∈𝒯c_{\ell}\in\mathcal{T} or a final response, after which the deterministic environment ℰ\mathcal{E} returns an observation oℓ=ℰ⁡(cℓ,hℓ)o_{\ell}=\mathcal{E}(c_{\ell},h_{\ell}) that is appended to the history. A rollout terminates when the agent emits a <response> block or the step budget is reached. For a teacher trajectory τ=(h0,a0,o0),…,(hL,aL)\tau=(h_{0},a_{0},o_{0}),\dots,(h_{L},a_{L}) the standard supervised fine-tuning objective factors as

ℒSFT(θ)=−∑ℓ=0L[logPθ(zℓ∣hℓ)+logPθ(cℓ∣hℓ,zℓ)],\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)=-\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\left[\log P_{\theta}(z_{\ell}\mid h_{\ell})+\log P_{\theta}(c_{\ell}\mid h_{\ell},z_{\ell})\right], (1)

with observation tokens masked from the loss, and for preference learning at a single step we follow DPO [6]:

ℒDPO​(θ)=−𝔼(h,a+,a−)​log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(a+∣h)πref​(a+∣h)−β​log⁡πθ​(a−∣h)πref​(a−∣h)),\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(h,a^{+},a^{-})}\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{+}\mid h)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{+}\mid h)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{-}\mid h)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{-}\mid h)}\right), (2)

where a+a^{+} is the teacher action and a−a^{-} is a synthetic hard negative produced in Stage C.

Tool environment.

We faithfully re-implement the seven-tool environment of OpenSearch-VL, matching its prompt format, tool schema, and observation tokenization; Table 9 in Appendix F lists every tool and backend. Retrieval tools are backed by SerpAPI [7]; the visual-restoration and cropping tools are implemented in Pillow and OpenCV, and OCR uses docTR [8]. The dispatcher maintains an img_N registry so that visual outputs of one tool can be referenced by index in subsequent calls, and every observation is wrapped in <observation>...</observation> matching the training-time tokenization exactly (required for stable inference).

Stage A: supervised distillation from released trajectories.

We download the 7-domain SearchVL-SFT-36k corpus (per-domain statistics: Table 3, Appendix B) and apply three preprocessing passes: compression strips the upstream chain-of-thought from tool observations and caps each cleaned observation at 4,000 characters, preserving the vast majority of observations end-to-end while removing roughly one third of total tokens; a deterministic per-trajectory hash produces a stratified 36,092 / 500 train / validation holdout split with all seven domains represented in both sides; and step expansion turns each LL-turn trajectory into LL prefix→\tonext-step records, yielding 133,439 step-level examples (a 3.65×\times expansion). We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B on Eq. (1) with LoRA adapters (rank r=16r=16, α=32\alpha=32) on the language tower, on a single eight-GPU node with mixed-precision DeepSpeed [9] ZeRO-3; the 8,192-token cutoff covers the full trajectory distribution at our observation cap, and one epoch over the 36,092 train trajectories at effective batch size 64 corresponds to 564 optimizer steps (2B SFT, 4B SFT). For a controlled comparison, 2B/4B Step-SFT instead train on the prefix→\tonext-step expansion, capped to the same optimizer steps and effective batch size with all other hyperparameters identical, isolating the supervision unit from data quantity and optimization budget.

Stage B: tool-distilled SFT.

Because the full seven-tool action space includes specialized image-restoration and OCR tools that are rarely invoked in the training distribution, we build a distilled variant in which the assistant may only call image_search, text_search, and crop: we rewrite the system prompt and tool schema to be substantially more compact, simplify the text_search argument set, and drop any trajectory (from the full 36,592-record corpus, train and validation combined) that used a disallowed tool, which removes 2,849 records (7.8%) and leaves 33,743. Re-running the same deterministic per-domain stratified split on this filtered pool, targeting a fixed validation size of 500 for direct comparability with Stage A, yields 33,243 train and 500 validation trajectories; this fresh stratified validation sample overlaps the Stage A validation set on 450 records (50 of the original 500 are dropped by the tool whitelist and replaced by surviving records). Everything else (LoRA rank, optimizer, batch size) matches Stage A except for a shorter 6,144-token cutoff enabled by the compact prompt (Table 8), so the effective difference is the action space and prompt surface (2B/4B 3-tool SFT).

Stage C: synthetic step-level preference optimization.

Real on-policy rollouts at training time would dominate the budget; instead we exploit the ∼\sim133K teacher decisions the preprocessed step-level corpus already provides. For each step we ask GPT-5 to synthesize hard negatives that a competent but imperfect small VLM would plausibly emit at that decision point, conditioned on the image and the prior history, partitioned into five interpretable failure modes: premature answer (a <response> before sufficient evidence), wrong tool (structurally inappropriate for the next step), weak query (right tool, unfocused or degenerate query), repeated query (duplicates a search already in context), and ignored image (ignores salient evidence in the registered img_N images). Every candidate is filtered through a programmatic validator with five checks—format, mode-specific structural rules (e.g. a wrong_tool negative must change the tool), absence of answer leakage relative to the gold response, absence of meta-language in the reasoning trace, and consistency of image references with the running registry; after tightening the generation prompt with two additional rules (stay in character and use only existing image handles), the audited issue rate dropped from 54%54\% to 0%0\% on a fixed sample of records (Appendix H). Running the validated pipeline over the full 133K step corpus yields 324,121 accepted preference pairs from ∼\sim96K teacher decisions (per-mode distribution in Figure 3, Appendix B); after dropping pairs beyond a length budget compatible with training memory (longer side ≤5,120\leq 5{,}120 tokens), we retain ∼\sim234K training and ∼\sim3K validation pairs (∼\sim73% of the full collection). Starting from each SFT checkpoint, we run DPO [6] with the sigmoid preference loss of Eq. (2) for one epoch over the filtered preference set at the SFT effective batch size (Table 8), using a relatively large β=0.3\beta=0.3 together with a small learning rate of 10−610^{-6}: the standard DPO recipe used on larger backbones (e.g. β=0.1\beta=0.1 with a ×10−65\!\times\!10^{-6} learning rate) collapsed the 2B model early in training, a related instability to the DPO failure mode documented in [10]. Final hyperparameters were selected by monitoring the reward gap on a held-out preference validation set (2B/4B SFT+DPO).

3 Evaluation Protocol

Benchmarks and inference.  We evaluate on four short-answer, knowledge-intensive multimodal benchmarks: FVQA [11] (59 questions from our held-out validation split, fvqa domain11 1 The fvqa domain contributes 60 records to the validation split (Table 3); one is excluded from the FVQA track because its image lacks a public URL required by the image_search tool, leaving 59 evaluated questions. These are OpenSearch-VL trajectories built over FVQA [11] images rather than items of the original FVQA test split, and are distinct from the FactualVQA set of MMSearch-R1 [12].), LiveVQA [13] (181 questions from our held-out validation split, livevqa domain), SimpleVQA [14] (500 questions sampled from the EN subset of m-a-p/SimpleVQA test), and VDR [15] (500 questions from Osilly/VDR-Bench-testmini; VDR-Bench is the Vision-DeepResearch benchmark of [15], distinct from the Vision-DeepResearch agent of [2]). Across the four benchmarks we evaluate ten model cells, each producing 1,240 agent rollouts for a total of 12,400 judged rollouts per evaluation pass. For each model we serve eight parallel single-GPU replicas with vLLM [16] and dispatch rollouts round-robin with light concurrency; the per-rollout step budget is MAX_STEPS = 5 unless stated otherwise, and the input image is downscaled to a maximum edge of 360 px before being passed to the model. Tool calls to the search backend are deduplicated through a persistent on-disk cache so that the same (tool, arguments) pair is paid for at most once across all ten model cells in an evaluation pass, reducing the per-pass search-API cost by roughly an order of magnitude.

LLM-as-judge and models compared.  We use GPT-5 as an LLM-as-judge: it sees the original benchmark image, the question, the reference answer, and the model’s final response, and must emit a strict JSON object with five fields: correct ∈{0,1}\in\{0,1\}, partially_correct ∈{0,1}\in\{0,1\} (mutually exclusive with correct=1), error_mode ∈\in {none, hallucinated, wrong_entity, missing_evidence, no_answer, partial, off_topic, other}, confidence ∈{0,1,2}\in\{0,1,2\}, and a one-sentence rationale (full prompt in Appendix G). The reported Pass@1 is the fraction with correct=1; the partial-credit rate is Pass@1+0.5⋅partial\text{Pass@1}+0.5\cdot\text{partial}. All 12,400 main-evaluation judgments parse successfully as JSON, and the judge’s self-rated confidence saturates at 2 on every judged row, so we treat it only as a pipeline-stability diagnostic (full discussion in Appendix C). Bootstrap confidence intervals over benchmark questions (Table 7, Appendix D) are our primary measure of result uncertainty; we recommend human spot-checking before treating any single judgment as ground truth. We compare ten model cells—the 2B and 4B variants of base, full-trajectory SFT, step-level SFT, 3-tool SFT, and SFT+DPO—but not the larger OpenSearch-VL 8B/30B/32B agents: the question we ask is whether 2B/4B agents can reach a useful operating point on a single eight-GPU node, not whether they overtake substantially larger frontier models (training-regime contrast: Table 4, Appendix B).

4 Results

Table 1 reports Pass@1 across all ten model cells and four benchmarks, visualized in Figure 1; partial-credit rates (Table 5) and bootstrap confidence intervals for the macro averages (Table 7) are deferred to Appendix D.22 2 Throughout the paper, stage-to-stage deltas (e.g. the +1.7-point DPO gain at 4B) are computed from unrounded scores before tabulation, so they can differ by 0.1 from differences of the rounded values printed in the tables.

(i) SFT transfers the agent contract, especially at 2B. The 2B base model fails primarily as an agent: it does not emit a usable <response> on 1,237 of 1,240 questions. Full-trajectory SFT cuts this failure mode to 514 cases and lifts macro Pass@1 to 28.4%; the corresponding lift on 4B is much smaller (+3.5 points). After this transfer, the 2B SFT model reaches the level of the 4B base on FVQA (64.4% vs. 61.0%), SimpleVQA (30.8% vs. 24.6%), and LiveVQA (16.6% vs. 16.0%) (per-stage gains: Figure 4(a), Appendix D).

(ii) Synthetic step-level DPO is a refinement, not the phase transition. On top of full-trajectory SFT, the synthetic DPO pairs add +1.0 average points on 2B and +1.7 average points on 4B. The largest localized delta is on FVQA at 4B (61.0 →\to 69.5, +8.5 points, corresponding to five additional correct answers out of 59), while LiveVQA at 4B loses 2.8 points relative to SFT. The macro confidence intervals in Table 7 overlap, so we interpret DPO as a directional refinement that can reduce some local decision errors.

(iii) Step-level SFT changes the terminal-behavior trade-off. On 2B, splitting the same trajectories into prefix→\tonext-step training units loses 1.5 average points relative to full-trajectory SFT and increases the no_answer count from 514 to 780; on 4B the same change gains 1.0 points, despite increasing no_answer from 587 to 682. Local transition supervision can help the larger backbone choose intermediate actions, but full-trajectory supervision more reliably teaches the small model the complete contract.

(iv) A compact tool interface is not automatically easier. Restricting the action interface to three tools is worse on 2B (–9.0 average points) but nearly free on 4B (–1.8 average points) and strictly better on FVQA, where 4B 3-tool SFT is the strongest cell at 71.2% Pass@1 (78.8% partial-credit). The error-mode pattern is consistent with a capacity-dependent trade-off: the 3-tool 4B model commits fewer wrong_entity mistakes than full-tool 4B SFT (242 vs. 298) but produces more no_answer failures (766 vs. 587).

Error modes. Table 6 and Figure 5 (Appendix D) aggregate the GPT-5 judge’s error_mode labels across all 1,240 judged questions per cell. The dominant qualitative effect of SFT is collapsing the no_answer pile of the base model into a roughly even split of correct and wrong_entity; DPO further reduces no_answer on 4B (587 →\to 511) and increases correct (248 →\to 254).

Step-budget ablation on VDR. VDR is the only benchmark in our suite where every model produces a large number of no_answer rollouts at MAX_STEPS=5 (59–70% for the four SFT and DPO checkpoints re-run below; higher still for the base models). To test whether the step cap binds or is merely a symptom, we re-ran the four SFT and DPO models on VDR alone with MAX_STEPS=8 (Table 2; Figure 6, Appendix D). The extra step budget reduces no_answer by roughly one third to one half on every model, but the additional rollouts mostly produce wrong_entity, not correct: the bottleneck for small agents on VDR is therefore not simply search depth but evidence verification; Appendix K.5 traces one rollout step by step.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

Where SFT helps and where it doesn’t.

The 2B base model is essentially non-functional as a search agent, emitting a final <response> on only 3 of 1,240 questions (one of them correct); SFT repairs this, but the resulting agent still produces wrong_entity on roughly 30% of questions, so entity grounding and evidence checking remain unsolved. The 4B base already follows the contract on many questions; SFT mostly polishes its tool selection.

Assessment of synthetic DPO.

The evidence supports a qualified version of the targeting claim: average Pass@1 grows on both backbones, with the cleanest single signal on 4B FVQA (+8.5 points) alongside a 13% reduction in no_answer over all four benchmarks (587 →\to 511, Table 6). Conversely, LiveVQA at 4B loses 2.8 points after DPO, and the 2B picture is closer to a redistribution than a uniform improvement: 2B SFT and 2B+DPO have nearly identical partial-credit rates (35.4 in both rows of Table 5). We therefore frame DPO as a refinement on top of SFT, not a substitute, with real on-policy preferences the natural next step; Appendix K walks through five paired case studies: the agent-contract transfer (K.1), three DPO improvement mechanisms (K.2–K.4), and a failure that survives DPO (K.5).

Tool space and backbone capacity.

The 3-tool ablation crystallizes a capacity-dependent trade-off: the full tool set adds cognitive overhead, while the compact tool set removes specialized operations needed by some questions; larger backbones appear more robust to the former but still lose coverage when OCR or perspective correction is actually required—so tool-surface design should be treated as a model-capacity choice rather than a fixed property of the environment.

What the VDR ablation says about agent design.

That three extra steps on VDR convert no_answer into wrong_entity rather than correct suggests that the limiting factor at small scales is not exploration but verification: the agent identifies the relevant region and retrieves plausible passages, but lacks a reliable habit of cross-checking the retrieved evidence against the question. A second-pass verification step, or a process reward model in the style of [17, 18], is a natural direction.

Reproducibility.

All ten model cells train with parameter-efficient LoRA on one eight-GPU node and are evaluated under the same agent environment and GPT-5 judge; we release training configurations, agent code, data pipelines, the judge prompt, and the search-cache schema (Appendix J).

Conclusion.

We presented LiteSearch-VL, a low-compute recipe for adapting Qwen3-VL-2B/4B into multimodal search agents from released teacher trajectories. Across four short-answer benchmarks and 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts, the main transfer is the agent contract—full-trajectory SFT changes the 2B model from almost never answering to 28.4% macro Pass@1—while compact tool distillation exposes a capacity-dependent trade-off and synthetic step-level DPO adds a smaller refinement (best 4B configuration: 30.8% macro Pass@1 and 37.1% partial-credit). The VDR ablation shows that extra search turns mainly convert abstentions into wrong-entity answers, pointing to verification-aware training as the next step.

Appendix A Related Work

Tool-augmented and agentic search.

WebGPT [19] demonstrated browser-assisted question answering with human feedback, and ReAct [20] popularized the think-then-act prompting pattern that interleaves natural-language reasoning with discrete tool calls; Toolformer [21] subsequently taught models to invoke tools in a self-supervised fashion. Search-R1 [22] introduced reinforcement learning with retrieval tokens masked out of the loss, and a number of multimodal search agents followed, including, in order of appearance, Visual-ARFT [23], MMSearch-R1 [12], WebWatcher [1], DeepMMSearch-R1 [24], DeepEyesV2 [25], SenseNova-MARS [26], and Vision-DeepResearch [2]. The most directly related effort is OpenSearch-VL [3], which released a 36K supervised-finetuning corpus of multi-turn agent trajectories together with an 8K reinforcement-learning prompt set, and trained 8B–32B Qwen3-VL backbones with a fatal-aware variant of GRPO [27]. Our work reuses the released data and tool schema, but targets a deliberately smaller and cheaper setting.

Parameter-efficient and preference-based post-training.

LoRA [28] and QLoRA [29] enable adapter-based fine-tuning of large backbones with a small fraction of trainable parameters. For preference alignment, DPO [6], ORPO [30], and SimPO [31] reduce the need for separate reward models, while Smaug [10] documents failure modes of DPO in which the likelihood of preferred completions declines during training. Step-DPO [32], process reward models [17, 18], and related work show that local, step-level preference signals can outperform trajectory-level rewards for long-horizon reasoning. Our synthetic step-level preference set adapts this perspective to multimodal agent rollouts, where each preference pair targets a single decision point inside a teacher trajectory.

Vision-language backbones and evaluation.

We build on Qwen3-VL [33] and the earlier Qwen2-VL [34]; alternative backbones include LLaVA [35], InternVL [36], and BLIP [37]. For evaluation we focus on benchmarks reported by OpenSearch-VL: FVQA [11], LiveVQA [13], SimpleVQA [14], VDR-Bench [15], MMSearch [38], and InfoSeek [39]; WebQA [40] contributes to the training corpus rather than to that evaluation suite (Table 3). We restrict ourselves to four short-answer benchmarks (FVQA, LiveVQA, SimpleVQA, VDR) that admit clean LLM-as-judge scoring and remain tractable at our compute budget. Training and serving use LlamaFactory [41], vLLM [16], and DeepSpeed [9].

Appendix B Pipeline Overview, Data Statistics, and Compute Footprint

This appendix collects the pipeline diagram, corpus statistics, synthetic-preference distribution, and compute-footprint comparison referenced from Sections 2 and 3.

Appendix C Judge Confidence Saturation

We verified directly against the raw judge logs that every judgment—all 12,400 main-evaluation rows, and all 14,400 rows once the four VDR step-budget ablation cells (Section 4) are included—reports confidence=2; the field never takes the value 0 or 1 anywhere in our data. We do not read this as evidence that every judgment is correct. Two properties of our setup make it plausible: (i) all four benchmarks use short factoid references (a name, date, or number), so deciding whether the model’s response matches the reference is usually a clear-cut string/entity comparison rather than a graded call, which is precisely the case our rubric (Appendix G) defines as confidence=2; and (ii) LLM self-rated confidence scores are known to saturate toward the top of a scale regardless of the rubric’s intended granularity. Because confidence is not used to filter, reweight, or otherwise affect any reported Pass@1, partial-credit, or error-mode number, this saturation does not bias our headline results, but it does mean the field carries no discriminative signal in our evaluation and should be read as a pipeline-stability diagnostic (JSON parses, a value is always emitted) rather than an independent reliability check.

Appendix D Additional Results Tables and Figures

Table 5 reports partial-credit rates for all ten model cells, Table 6 the full error-mode distributions, Table 7 the bootstrap confidence intervals for the macro averages, Figure 4 the per-stage gains (Figure 4(a)) and the macro averages across all five regimes for both backbones (Figure 4(b)), Figure 5 the stacked error-mode distributions, and Figure 6 the VDR step-budget ablation, all deferred from Section 4.

Appendix E Hyperparameters and Compute

Table 8 lists the training hyperparameters for every training run; its five rows cover four distinct configurations, since the 2B and 4B SFT runs differ only in backbone. SFT runs on a single eight-GPU node with mixed-precision DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, and DPO runs on a single eight-GPU node with ZeRO-2. Backbones, LoRA configuration, and effective batch size are kept identical across stages to enable clean comparisons.

All SFT runs use LoRA with rank r=16r=16 and scale α=32\alpha=32, dropout 0.050.05, applied to all linear projections of the language tower. The vision tower is frozen; the multimodal projector is trainable. We use cosine learning-rate schedules with 3% warmup, gradient checkpointing, and image inputs are clipped to a maximum of 65,536 pixels (approximately 256×256256\times 256) during training.

For DPO we use the sigmoid preference loss with β=0.3\beta=0.3 and a small learning rate of 10−610^{-6}; the standard recipe (β=0.1\beta=0.1, learning rate ×10−65\!\times\!10^{-6}) was unstable on the 2B backbone, a related instability to the DPO failure mode discussed in [10]. The reference model is the corresponding SFT checkpoint.

Appendix F Tool Environment

Table 9 summarizes the seven distinct tools exposed to the agent; web_search is dispatched as an alias of text_search, giving eight callable names. The full tool schema and JSON argument signatures are released with the code. The dispatcher maintains an img_N registry across turns; visual tools return a new img_N+1 reference and the original training format wraps every observation in <observation>Tool execution result:\n...\n</observation>.

Appendix G GPT-5 Judge Prompt

The judge receives the benchmark image, the question, the reference answer, and the model response. The system rubric is reproduced verbatim below.

⬇
You are a strict but fair grader for a multimodal question-answering
benchmark. You will see the original image (above this prompt), a
QUESTION, a REFERENCE answer (ground truth), and a MODEL response.
Compare the MODEL response to the REFERENCE answer for that QUESTION
about that IMAGE, and emit a structured JSON judgment with five fields.
Scoring rules:
1. ‘correct = 1‘ iff the MODEL response gives the SAME substantive
answer as the REFERENCE. Tolerate phrasing, length, capitalization,
formatting differences. Extra background prose is fine if the core
answer is present and consistent.
2. ‘correct = 0‘ if the model’s answer is missing, contradicts the
reference, identifies the wrong entity/date/number, or is so vague
it cannot be matched.
3. ‘partially_correct = 1‘ iff ‘correct = 0‘ AND the model got the
primary entity / key subject right but missed or contradicted a
secondary attribute (e.g. correct person but wrong year; correct
landmark but wrong height). Otherwise 0. If ‘correct = 1‘, set 0.
4. For factoid answers (names, dates, numbers, places): the substantive
token must appear and must agree with the REFERENCE (allow obvious
spelling / transliteration variants).
5. ‘error_mode‘ is one of: ’none’ (when correct=1), ’hallucinated’
(fabricated facts), ’wrong_entity’ (named wrong subject),
’missing_evidence’ (plausible answer but no real grounding),
’no_answer’ (empty / refused / truncated before answer), ’partial’
(got main entity but missed a sub-detail - pair with
partially_correct=1), ’off_topic’ (answered a different question),
’other’.
6. ‘confidence‘ is your own confidence in this judgment: 2 = obvious,
1 = required some interpretation, 0 = genuinely ambiguous.
7. Ignore the model’s reasoning trace, tool calls, and markup - only
the final answer content matters.
8. Output STRICT JSON ONLY, no markdown fences, no extra text, exactly:
{"correct": 0|1, "partially_correct": 0|1,
"error_mode": "<one of the 8 modes>", "confidence": 0|1|2,
"rationale": "<one sentence>"}

The per-item prompt then appends the question, reference, and truncated model response in three labeled sections and ends with the directive Return STRICT JSON only.

Appendix H Synthetic Preference Generator

For each step record in the corpus, the generator receives the input image, the conversation prefix, the teacher’s actual next step (the chosen action), and the gold final answer (used only for leak detection). For each applicable failure mode it asks GPT-5 to produce a plausible, hard, in-character alternative action that a competent but imperfect small VLM might emit. The system prompt enforces eight hard rules:

⬇
1. Stay in character. The thought must read as if the model believes
the chosen action is correct. Do NOT betray the mistake with
meta-language such as "even though", "instead of doing the right
thing", "I might mistakenly", "for this exercise".
2. Use only existing image handles. Image-consuming tools must
reference a ‘img_N‘ that appears in the prior history. Do NOT
fabricate filenames or URLs.
3. Respect the tool schema. The tool name must be one of the allowed
tools; arguments must match the JSON schema.
4. Match the requested failure mode structurally. For example, a
‘wrong_tool‘ action must change the tool name vs. the chosen
action; a ‘weak_query‘ action must keep the same tool; a
‘repeated_query‘ action must share at least one bag-of-words
match with a prior call.
5. Do NOT leak the gold answer. The rejected action must not contain
the gold final answer string or any obvious paraphrase.
6. Keep the format. The action must be a contiguous
<think>...</think><tool_call>{...}</tool_call> block, or
<think>...</think><response>...</response> for the
‘premature_answer‘ mode.
7. Be hard. The rejected action should be the kind of mistake a real
small model would make, not a strawman.
8. Output strict JSON keyed by mode; one entry per applicable mode.

A programmatic validator (format / mode-specific rules / answer leak / meta-language leak / image argument sanity) drops any entry that violates a rule before it is written to the final pair file. After adding the stay in character and existing image handles only rules, the audited issue rate dropped from 54%54\% to 0%0\% on a fixed sample of records (Section 2).

Appendix I Per-Domain Validation Statistics

For completeness, Table 10 reports the per-domain composition of the held-out validation set, including the two domains (fvqa, livevqa) that we promote to standalone benchmark tracks.

Appendix J Reproducibility Checklist

  • •

    Code and configs. All ten model cells in Table 1 are produced by configuration files that share a common template; the only differences are the base model, the dataset, and the training stage.

  • •

    Data pipeline. The preprocessing script rebuilds the train / validation split and the step-level expansion deterministically given a fixed seed.

  • •

    Tool environment. The agent loop, tool dispatcher, and search cache are shared across the interactive playground and the evaluation harness, ensuring identical inference behavior.

  • •

    Judge. The GPT-5 judge prompt is fixed (Appendix G) and applied identically to every model; the judge’s self-rated confidence field is 2 (the maximum) on every individual judged row, not merely on average per cell. We do not treat this as a reliability guarantee — see the discussion in Section 3 for why we believe this reflects the clear-cut nature of factoid matching in our benchmarks rather than a well-calibrated confidence signal.

  • •

    Caching. Search-API results are cached on disk and shared across all ten model cells in a single evaluation pass; error-shaped observations are not cached.

Appendix K Qualitative Case Studies

This appendix presents five rollouts drawn directly from the evaluation harness to illustrate, on real questions, what each training stage changes about agent behavior. Each case includes the benchmark question, the gold reference answer, a brief image description, the trajectory of each model side by side, the model’s final answer, and the GPT-5 judge’s verdict. Trajectories are excerpted from eval_outputs/<model>/<benchmark>/responses.jsonl; long <think> blocks, tool observations, and intermediate tool calls are elided with “[…]” for readability, and the text shown is otherwise unmodified. The first four cases study stage-wise progress (Base →\to SFT, and three mechanisms by which DPO improves over SFT at 2B and 4B); the final case studies a failure mode that survives DPO: the verification bottleneck on VDR (Section 4).

K.1 Case 1: SFT teaches the agent contract (2B Base →\to 2B SFT)

Setup.

Benchmark: FVQA, item fvqa_002606. The image shows a branch of an ornamental shrub bearing clusters of small, pink, winged seed pods against a blurred green background (Figure 7).

Question.

“What is the name of this plant with pink seed pods?”

Reference.

Dodonaea viscosa (commonly known as hop-bush or hopseed bush).

Qwen3-VL-2B Base.

The base model executes the right tools in the right order and even drafts a correct identification sentence, but never wraps its answer in a <response> block, so the harness records no_answer.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of this plant with pink seed pods?
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "image_search",
"arguments": {"url": "img_1"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [{’title’: ’wedge-leaf hop-bush (Logan RE 12.8.20 Flora) -
iNaturalist’, ’source’: ’iNaturalist’},
{’title’: ’AALII ...’, ’source’: ’...’}, ...]
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "wedge-leaf hop-bush plant name"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: Dodonaea viscosa URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Dodonaea_viscosa Summary: Dodonaea viscosa, also known
as the broadleaf hopbush ...
[assistant] The plant with the pink seed pods is the wedge-leaf hop-bush,
also known as Dodonaea viscosa ...
[stop] No <tool_call> and no <response> found -- ending loop.
Final response: (empty)
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, error_mode=no_answer.

Qwen3-VL-2B SFT.

The same backbone after one epoch of full-trajectory SFT runs the same two-step search chain, but now closes the rollout with a properly formatted <response>.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of this plant with pink seed pods?
[assistant] <think>Pink winged seed capsules on a green-leaf branch;
image_search should identify the species.</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "image_search",
"arguments": {"url": "img_1"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [{’title’: ’wedge-leaf hop-bush (Logan RE 12.8.20 Flora)’,
’source’: ’iNaturalist’}, ...]
[assistant] <think>Hop-bush is the working hypothesis; confirm the
scientific name with text_search.</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "wedge-leaf hop-bush scientific name"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: Dodonaea viscosa URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Dodonaea_viscosa ...
[assistant] <response>The plant with the pink seed pods is Dodonaea
viscosa, commonly known as the Wedge-Leaf Hop Bush or
Broadleaf Hop Bush ...</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=1, error_mode=none.

Interpretation.

Both rollouts retrieve the same evidence; only the SFT model has internalized the contract that a final <response> block is mandatory. This is the dominant qualitative effect of full-trajectory SFT on 2B and the source of the jump from 0.1% to 28.4% macro Pass@1 reported in Section 4.

K.2 Case 2: DPO recovers tool use on 2B (2B SFT →\to 2B DPO)

Setup.

Benchmark: FVQA, item fvqa_004100. The image is a circular football-club crest with the words “Ekranas” and “Futbolo Klubas” around a stylized white “E” (Figure 8).

Question.

“What is the name of the football club shown in the image?”

Reference.

FK Ekranas, a Lithuanian football club (Futbolo Klubas Ekranas).

Qwen3-VL-2B SFT.

The 2B SFT model skips tool use entirely. It commits to an answer from raw perception alone, misreading the Lithuanian word “Futbolo Klubas” as Bulgarian/Cyrillic and inventing a fictitious Bulgarian club. The judge marks the answer partial because the entity name is right but the geographic attribution is wrong.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of the football club shown in the image?
[assistant] <think>Circular crest with text I read as Cyrillic
"EKranas / Futbolo Klubas".</think>
<response>The football club shown in the image is Ekranas
Futbolo Klubas (Bulgarian football club, based in Plovdiv) ...
</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, partial=1, error_mode=partial -- correct entity,
wrong country / city.

Qwen3-VL-2B DPO.

The DPO checkpoint invokes the tool chain that the SFT model skipped: it identifies the crest with image_search, then issues a text_search for confirmation, and emits a correct <response> attributing the club to Lithuania.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of the football club shown in the image?
[assistant] <think>[...]</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "image_search",
"arguments": {"url": "img_1"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [{’title’: ’FK Ekranas - Wikipedia’, ’source’: ’Wikipedia’},
{’title’: ’FK Ekranas 2025-26 Squad - ESPN (IN)’,
’source’: ’ESPN’}, ...]
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "FK Ekranas football club"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: FK Ekranas URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
FK_Ekranas Summary: Ekranas is a Lithuanian football club ...
[assistant] <response>The football club shown in the image is FK Ekranas
(Futbolo Klubas Ekranas), a Lithuanian football club based in
Panevezys ...</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=1, error_mode=none.

Interpretation.

The 2B SFT model exhibits the premature answer failure mode that the synthetic hard-negative classes target directly (Section 2): it commits from raw perception without invoking any tool. DPO shifts the same backbone toward the evidence-then-answer contract.

K.3 Case 3: DPO closes the loop on a multi-tool rollout (4B SFT →\to 4B DPO)

Setup.

Benchmark: SimpleVQA, item simplevqa_1057. The image is a Costco retail wine display showing three shelf price tags: Northstar Merlot (Columbia Valley, 3.0 L) at $139.99, Moët & Chandon Impérial (1.5 L) at $114.99, and Chateau Ste. Michelle Cold Creek Cabernet (Columbia Valley, 3.0 L) at $109.99. The question asks only about the Merlot and Cabernet tags (Figure 9).

Question.

“What is the total price for a bottle of Merlot and a bottle of Cabernet shown in the image?”

Reference.

$249.98.

Qwen3-VL-4B SFT.

The SFT model chains several image-processing and search tools—crop, super_resolution, and finally text_search—never produces a final answer, and exhausts the step budget.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the total price for a bottle of Merlot and a
bottle of Cabernet shown in the image?
[...]
[assistant] <think>Crop the top of the image to isolate the price tags.</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "crop",
"arguments": {"image": "img_1", "x": 0, "y": 0,
"width": 300, "height": 200}}</tool_call>
[observation] Image cropped successfully. New image ID: img_2. ...
[assistant] <think>[...]</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "super_resolution",
"arguments": {"image": "img_2", "scale": 4}}</tool_call>
[observation] Super resolution enhancement completed. New image ID: img_3. ...
[...]
[assistant] <think>[...]</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "Costco Merlot Cabernet price"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: A $13.99 Costco Wine Find ...
[stop] Hit max_steps=5 without a <response>.
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, error_mode=no_answer.

Qwen3-VL-4B DPO.

The DPO checkpoint crops the price-tag region, re-reads the two visible prices from the cropped image ($139.99 and $109.99), runs a sanity-check text_search, and commits to a correct final answer with arithmetic.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the total price for a bottle of Merlot and a
bottle of Cabernet shown in the image?
[assistant] <think>Crop the top-left price tag region to read the prices
directly.</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "crop",
"arguments": {"image": "img_1", "x": 0, "y": 0,
"width": 300, "height": 200}}</tool_call>
[observation] Image cropped successfully. New image ID: img_2. ...
[assistant] <think>From img_2 I can read: MERLOT $139.99, CABERNET
$109.99. Sanity-check with text_search before committing.
</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "Costco Merlot Cabernet store price"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: Total Wine & More ...
[assistant] <response>Based on the image, the prices are Merlot $139.99
and Cabernet $109.99. The total is $139.99 + $109.99 = $249.98.
\boxed{249.98}</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=1, error_mode=none.

Interpretation.

The two failure modes the SFT model exhibits here—wrong tool (chaining super_resolution on top of crop instead of reading the visible prices) and repeated query (re-asking the same visual question without committing to the visible numbers)—are exactly the categories targeted by the synthetic step-DPO negatives (Section 2). The DPO checkpoint commits earlier and uses the visible image evidence: it crops once, reads the prices, and writes the final answer. This is the multi-tool source of the SimpleVQA improvements visible in Table 1.

K.4 Case 4: DPO avoids over-specification (4B SFT-partial →\to 4B DPO-correct)

Setup.

Benchmark: FVQA, item fvqa_004018. The image shows a steel-arch road bridge spanning a tropical waterway, with green hills in the background (Figure 10).

Question.

“In which year did this bridge officially open?”

Reference.

1962 (the Bridge of the Americas / Puente de las Américas, Panama, officially opened on October 12, 1962).

Qwen3-VL-4B SFT.

The model retrieves correct evidence identifying the Bridge of the Americas in Panama and the opening year 1962. It then over-specifies: instead of stopping at the requested year, it inserts a fabricated exact date (“October 2, 1962”) taken from a partial reading of the search passage. The judge marks the answer as partial because the year is right but the day is wrong by ten days.

⬇
[user] <image>In which year did this bridge officially open?
[assistant] <think>Steel-arch road bridge over a tropical channel; identify
via image_search.</think>
<tool_call>{"name": "image_search",
"arguments": {"url": "img_1"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [{’title’: ’Ficheiro:PuenteAmericas3.jpg - Wikipedia, a
enciclopedia libre’, ’source’: ’Wikipedia’},
{’title’: ’The Bridge of the Americas is a road bridge
in Panama ...’, ’source’: ’Alamy’}, ...]
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "Bridge of the Americas Panama opening
year"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: Bridge of the Americas
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_of_the_Americas
Summary: ... officially opened on October 12, 1962 ...
[assistant] <response>This is the Bridge of the Americas (Puente de las
Americas) in Panama. According to historical records, this
bridge officially opened on October 2, 1962 ...</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, partial=1, error_mode=partial -- correct bridge
and year, but wrong specific day.

Qwen3-VL-4B DPO.

The DPO checkpoint executes the same two tool calls but answers at the granularity the question actually requests, dropping the unrequested day-level detail.

⬇
[user] <image>In which year did this bridge officially open?
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "image_search",
"arguments": {"url": "img_1"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [{’title’: ’The Bridge of the Americas is a road bridge in
Panama ...’, ’source’: ’Alamy’}, ...]
[assistant] <tool_call>{"name": "text_search",
"arguments": {"q": "Bridge of the Americas Panama opening
year"}}</tool_call>
[observation] [Passage 1] Title: Bridge of the Americas Summary:
Completed in 1962 at a cost of US$20 million ...
[assistant] <response>This is the Bridge of the Americas (Puente de las
Americas) in Panama. It officially opened in 1962 ...
</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=1, error_mode=none.

Interpretation.

The SFT model adds a specific date that the question does not ask for and that does not survive scrutiny. The DPO checkpoint terminates at the granularity supported by the question and the retrieved evidence. This is the same answer-fidelity mechanism the synthetic step-DPO negatives target through the premature answer and ignored image classes (Section 2): the pre-DPO model is willing to elaborate beyond what evidence justifies, while the post-DPO model stays inside the supported envelope. This pattern contributes to the +1.7 average-point gain at 4B (Section 4).

K.5 Case 5: A failure that survives DPO — verification on VDR

Setup.

Benchmark: VDR, item vdr_base_Nature_833. The image is an overhead photo of a garden bed; at the top is a leafy plant forming a rosette of broad, spear-shaped leaves, with a small blue forget-me-not flower and seedlings nearby (Figure 11).

Question.

“What is the name of the plant at the top with broad, spear-shaped leaves?”

Reference.

Coreopsis.

Qwen3-VL-4B SFT.

The SFT model crops the leaf rosette, then guesses a different species in each search (forget-me-not, then columbine) without ever committing to a final answer, and exhausts the step budget.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of the plant at the top with broad,
spear-shaped leaves?
[...]
[assistant] <think>Crop the top rosette to inspect the leaves.</think>
<tool_call>crop(img_1, x=100, y=0, width=300, height=200)</tool_call>
[observation] Image cropped successfully. New image ID: img_2. ...
[...]
[assistant] <tool_call>text_search("plant spear-shaped leaves garden bed
forget-me-not companion plant")</tool_call>
[observation] ...
[assistant] <tool_call>text_search("Columbine plant spear-shaped leaves
garden bed")</tool_call>
[observation] ...
[stop] Hit max_steps=5 without a <response>.
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, error_mode=no_answer.

Qwen3-VL-4B DPO.

The DPO checkpoint commits early, but to a confident misidentification: it names Broadleaf Plantain (Plantago major) — a plausible visual match for a broad-leaved rosette, but the wrong species.

⬇
[user] <image>What is the name of the plant at the top with broad,
spear-shaped leaves?
[...]
[assistant] <tool_call>text_search("garden plant broad spear-shaped leaves
dandelion plantain identification")</tool_call>
[observation] ...
[assistant] <response>The plant at the top with broad, spear-shaped leaves
is Broadleaf Plantain (Plantago major), also commonly known as
Common Plantain ...</response>
GPT-5 judge: correct=0, error_mode=wrong_entity.

Interpretation.

DPO has done its job in one sense (no_answer →\to a committed answer), but the answer is a plausible-but-wrong species: the DPO model seeds its search with a guessed identity (“dandelion plantain”) and commits to the first plausible match without cross-checking the leaf morphology against the true species. This is the canonical instance of the verification bottleneck identified in Section 4: on multi-hop deep-research questions, additional search turns reliably convert no_answer into wrong_entity rather than into correct. Closing this gap requires a verification-style signal that the current SFT and synthetic-DPO recipes do not provide.

Appendix L Broader Impacts

Making tool-using multimodal search agents workable at 2B–4B parameters lowers the compute and cost barrier to deploying them, which is broadly useful for on-device and low-resource settings and is the motivation for this work. The same accessibility carries a risk that our own error analysis makes concrete: the resulting agents retrieve real web evidence yet still commit confidently to a wrong primary entity on a substantial fraction of questions (Section 4, Appendix K), and the VDR ablation shows that giving them more search turns converts abstentions into confident errors rather than correct answers. Deployments should therefore not treat these agents’ answers as verified, and we identify verification-aware training as the priority for future work. We release no new model weights or scraped corpora with this submission.
